utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-84-T, the Prosecutor versus Ramush Haradinaj et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. I first would like to inform the parties that since I yesterday had failed to instruct the witness not to speak with anyone about his testimony, with the assistance of one of our interpreters I told the witness just outside the court not any other thing but just the instruction as I usually give to witnesses. This is just that it be on the record. Then, Mr. Hasanaj, I would like you -- to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you gave at the beginning of your testimony yesterday, that is that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Mr. Re, you indicated yesterday that you might have concluded your examination-in-chief, but not for certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I have a few moments -- a few minutes left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A few minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hasanaj, Mr. Re will continue his examination. Please proceed Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Hasanaj. There's just a few matters I want to ask you about your --

utterances.speaker: ZYMER HASANAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Good afternoon. About your evidence yesterday. In your -- excuse me. Yesterday you were explaining to the Trial Chamber that there was this expression, an Albanian expression, you called it a wise saying: "The children eat the fruit in the trees and the parents get sore teeth." Yesterday the Judge in the middle, Judge Orie, asked if you could provide a -- an explanation of what it means so that everyone in the court knows what this Albanian saying means.

utterances.speaker: ZYMER HASANAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said that, and I meant my son, who at that moment went there, and because of that I have these challenges in front of me. I have -- I had to come here to this courtroom and testify. That's what I meant. Because if my son had not been there to see what he saw, Mr. Balaj would have known himself who that person was, and he knows today.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Does that satisfactorily explain it to the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I asked yesterday -- one of the interpreters, as a matter of fact, gave me an explanation spontaneously after court and said that the origin of this saying is that children starting picking and eating fruit when they're not ripe yet, that then the parents, of course, have to deal with the sore teeth of the children as a consequence of their behaviour. That's how it was explained to me, and I think the matter has been sufficiently dealt with. The witness explained what it meant to him, and this seems to be the background of this saying. You understood what I just said? That's your understanding as well of the origin of this saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can we just display a section of the statement in Sanction, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In your statement, you referred to -- this is at paragraph 20, a person called Ahmet Ukaj being concerned and distressed and telling you that Galani was one of the persons in the forest who had killed a woman. That's the woman we now know is Sanije Balaj. My question is simply this: Are you related to Ahmet Ukaj? And if so, what is your relationship?

utterances.speaker: ZYMER HASANAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are cousins. We are from the same village, from Vranoc e Vogel. And at that moment, we went together there. And he was protecting my son when we went there, because he was afraid that somebody would shoot. And I think he stayed there about an hour after I left. And after he came back to me, he was very distressed and said those words to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And the same with in paragraph 17, you referred to Hysen Ukaj and Sokol Tolaj. Is Hysen Ukaj also one of your cousins and what is his relationship to Ahmet Ukaj?

utterances.speaker: ZYMER HASANAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hysen Ukaj is a close relative to Ahmet. To me they're the same approximately, and they are from the same village as me. Sokol Tolaj was somebody who had left his village because of the war and had come to live in our village. I went home with Sokol and Hysen and Ahmet stayed behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And also in your statement at paragraph 22, you refer to understanding that Shaban Balaj, who testified yesterday, went to the house of Mete Krasniqi and the Balaj family told Mete, "You are the one who took the girl. I am telling you to bring her back." Mete Krasniqi, is he deceased?

utterances.speaker: ZYMER HASANAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mete Krasniqi died after the war and the Balaj family and Shaban Balaj himself went to Mete Krasniqi and asked for the body of his sister to be given to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yesterday I asked you about the Serb attack on your village on the 29th of May, and I asked you how many were on either side; that is, the Serbian side and the KLA side. And you said: "We were very few in numbers." I just want you to, if you can - I know it's been a long time - tell the Trial Chamber approximately how few you mean by "very few in numbers."

utterances.speaker: ZYMER HASANAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said this yesterday, and maybe you misinterpreted it. As I said, there were very few of us and we were not mobilised to put up a resistance against the Serbs. There were very few of us as members of the KLA, and our main concern was for our families to get to a safe place as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm just after numbers. When you say "very few," are you talking about five, ten, fifteen? 100, 200? Three people? Just approximately, how many KLA fighters were there?

utterances.speaker: ZYMER HASANAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. I couldn't give you an exact figure. I suppose the Court would like an exact figure, but I cannot give you one. We were about ten, fifteen. We just wanted to leave to go to a safe place.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And what were the ten/fifteen of you armed with?

utterances.speaker: ZYMER HASANAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had light weapons. Somebody had a semiautomatic rifle. Somebody else a Kalashnikov. Simple light weapons. What could we do with those kinds of weapons?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you remember whether you had uniforms?

utterances.speaker: ZYMER HASANAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have a uniform. Other people did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I want to clarify one of your answers yesterday. In describing what the Serbs did, you said: "They set fire to the village. More than half the houses in the village. They killed some, as I said. They killed livestock. They destroyed everything they could. As I said, four persons were burned." Now, what we've got written down is you said four persons were burned. Are you referring to houses or people?

utterances.speaker: ZYMER HASANAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not houses but people were charred in the houses that got burned. Three were burnt and one of them was killed by a shell launched by a tank. He was in the forest in Lugu i Isufit. That's where he was killed. His name was Imer Kukaj [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How many military casualties were there on either side? That is, KLA side or Serbian side?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I think the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- characterisation of KLA side and military casualties may be too much. You can speak about how many casualty there is were and get further definition there, but question is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps on your side and the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If that would do, Mr. Re. There may have been more parties involved. I think it would have been understood this way. But casualties -- could you tell us about the number of casualties.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On our side, the Albanian side, there were four casualties. Three were burnt in their own homes, and the other one, the fourth one, was killed. But there were other damages as well caused in livestock and crops. I don't know about any casualties on the part of the Serbs. We could not know, because we could not go to them or approach them and ask them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The four people who were killed, were they fighters for the KLA or were they civilians?

utterances.speaker: ZYMER HASANAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: None of them were KLA fighters. All of them were civilians. One woman and three men.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I want to show you two photographs and ask you whether you can identify the area shown in the two photographs. Can the witness firstly be shown 65 ter 2070 at page 2. Can you see the photograph clearly on the screen, or do you want me to give you a -- a copy of the photograph in hard copy?

utterances.speaker: ZYMER HASANAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you recognise that?

utterances.speaker: ZYMER HASANAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this is the place where the attack on Vranoc occurred. It's the hill, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Is this the area of Lugu i Isufit where you went with your relatives on the day that Sanije Balaj was killed? Is that area shown in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: ZYMER HASANAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. It's that area, yes. Not the hill that I mentioned earlier, because the hill was the place where the Serbs were positioned. This is the part called Zarki Pojas.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: May that be received into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's P925, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. No objections? Then it's admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The second photograph I'm going to show you is 65 ter 2070, page 1. That, too, will come up on the screen. In your statement, you referred to a water spring in the area of Lugu i Isufit. Does that photograph show the water spring which you referred to in your statement, which was in the area around near where Sanije Balaj was killed?

utterances.speaker: ZYMER HASANAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can't see the exact water spring, but this is the area. This is the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: May that also be received into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would there be any objection against having them together under one exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Not from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objection? Then this photograph will join the other one, which was, as far as I remember, P925. Two photographs now in P925, both admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's the evidence in chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Emmerson, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Hasanaj, you'll now be cross-examined first by Mr. Emmerson, who's counsel for Mr. Haradinaj. Please proceed, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Mr. Hasanaj, I have one or two questions for you from this side of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hasanaj, perhaps you'll look at Mr. Emmerson who's standing there, who's putting the questions now.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Just one or two questions for you, if I may, please. Your village was Vranoc e Vogel; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZYMER HASANAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness be asked to sit closer to the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you assist the witness and ... Could you please come closer to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And the other village of Vranoc or with the name of Vranoc was called Vranoc e Madhe, M-a-d-h-e; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZYMER HASANAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Din Krasniqi, did he live in Vranoc e Vogel or Vranoc e Madhe?

utterances.speaker: ZYMER HASANAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Vranoc e Madhe.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Do you know a man called Cufe Krasniqi or did you at the time know a man called Cufe Krasniqi?

utterances.speaker: ZYMER HASANAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, yesterday you testified - and I'm looking at page 8720, line 17 for those who are following - you gave evidence yesterday in these terms. You said: "Ramush Haradinaj didn't appoint Din Krasniqi. It was the people who elected him." And we have heard some evidence, as you know, from Shaban Balaj to the same effect. We've also heard testimony from a man called Cufe Krasniqi that it was he who suggested Din Krasniqi as commander. Do you remember the process of election in the villages by which Din Krasniqi came to be elected?

utterances.speaker: ZYMER HASANAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you yesterday that I am from Vranoc e Vogel, Deqan municipality. However, I joined the Vranoc e Madhe staff later on, when Din Krasniqi was elected. Din Krasniqi was elected commander of the village at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And he was elected, was he, by the local villagers from the area --

utterances.speaker: ZYMER HASANAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from the villagers.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, there's just one other topic I wanted to clarify with you briefly, if I may, and it relates to the account that your son Durim gave you on the day that you went to the area of Lugu i Isufit. Now, in your witness statement in this case, you've described how you came home that day and spoke first to your wife and then to your son about what it is that your son had witnessed; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZYMER HASANAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, I just want to be clear about one detail. We have a witness statement that your son Durim made to the Prosecution about this, in which he describes having seen not one man and a woman out of a car but two men, both out of the car, trying to force the woman out. And I see in your witness statement at paragraph 16 you say in terms that the boy told you that on their way back, they saw two men with a woman and that he had seen the two men forcing the woman out of the vehicle. Is that your recollection?

utterances.speaker: ZYMER HASANAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Those are my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Emmerson. One question for you. Did I miss something you said? That the witness would be -- know that Shaban Balaj gave evidence to the same effect? I missed why this witness would --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry -- sorry, what I was indicating was that the witness -- this witness would know that Shaban Balaj had testified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, so not covering the whole of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Another way of that, but That is --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think that because he made reference in his evidence in chief to the fact that we had heard from Shaban Balaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then that has been -- is on the record now. Mr. Guy-Smith. Mr. Guy-Smith is Defence counsel for Mr. Balaj, Mr. Hasanaj, and he'll now put further questions to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: ZYMER HASANAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I have but a few questions to ask you, and they relate to the testimony you gave yesterday. You said yesterday that you knew that Idriz Balaj had been gaoled for the first time, and my question to you is: Is that as a result of the trial in Kosovo in 2002, the Dukagjin trial?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you receive interpretation, Mr. Hasanaj? Because I --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please answer the question whether--

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't know Idriz Balaj before, but after the war I heard that Idriz Balaj and Togeri are one and the same person, and this is what I stated in my statement. But I didn't know him, nor did I ever meet him, so I know nothing about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you very much. 1-6R7B8G9 is that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that -- is that an answer to your question, Mr. Guy-Smith?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It's not directly an answer to my question. I can get the answer to the question too. In addition, I think that probably -- probably resolves it, but I can ask the -- the question again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure. No problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm left with a puzzlement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: After the war, Mr. Balaj was involved in a trial in Dukagjin. Are you aware of him being involved in that trial?

utterances.speaker: ZYMER HASANAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only heard that he was in gaol. I don't know more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you had indicated yesterday -- when you said yesterday after he was in gaol the first time, you were referring to him being in gaol as a result of what happened at the Dukagjin trial; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZYMER HASANAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you once again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Guy-Smith. Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I have no questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Re, any need to put further questions to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. There's just one matter in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I would like to perhaps first seek a clarification on another matter, so that you can include that. I don't know whether there's any need to that at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hasanaj, the Chamber has read your statement. There's a tiny little matter I'd like to ask you about. In paragraph 2 of your statement, you said: "We considered ourselves to be KLA but we did not have a commander as such. We obtained a few weapons as well as some military attire with the KLA insignia for the first time when a headquarters was established in Vranoc e Madhe around the 15th of April, 1998." You also said in paragraph 3 of your statement: "We obtained weapons for the first time when I sent two people from my village along with another seven or eight others from Vranoc e Madhe to Albania." So you describe -- and you say that that was sometime after the Serb attack on your village on the 29th of May. So you say for the first time you obtained weapons at the end of March, a few weapons, and then you said for the first times we got weapons from Albania but then you say this was after the attack on the 29th of May. Now, I understood your statement to say that you got a few weapons for the first time in March 1998 and then that after the 29th of May, you for the first time got a larger quantity of weapons which is described in your statement, coming from Albania, where you sent several people. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: ZYMER HASANAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct. It's true. Do you want me to explain it further?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, if -- if -- of course, I was puzzled by "the first time", which you used two times, and of course "the first time" can only be once. Therefore I understood "the first time" initially to say just a few weapons; and "the first time" in paragraph 3 to say the first time that we went to gather weapons from Albania and then you describe that this was a Kalashnikovs, mortars, anti-attack rocket, sniper rifles. Is that how I have to understand your statement?

utterances.speaker: ZYMER HASANAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Hasanaj, I just want to ask you to clarify something in relation to a question Mr. Emmerson over there asked you. Now, he asked you about the local villagers electing Din Krasniqi. Can you just refer to your statement, paragraph 4 in your statement there. Can that please be displayed in English in Sanction while the witness looks at his hard copy there. You can see the second sentence in paragraph 4, where you said that "Ramush came to announce the appointment of Din Krasniqi as the commander of that area in mid-April." And then you say: "Three representatives had been sent from our village to Gllogjan to ask Ramush's approval for this appointment." Now, was the reason for their going to Gllogjan, is that in the next sentence, where it says: "Ramush was understood to be the zone commander of Dukagjini Valley, meaning that he gave orders to the commanders of the villages"?

utterances.speaker: ZYMER HASANAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe I just guessed. I don't remember it very accurately. I only know that Din Krasniqi was elected by the co-villagers and that that is the Peje commune. The three people that went there, this is something that I heard about. I heard that three people had gone to Ramush Haradinaj. As to whether they met him or not and how the question of Din Krasniqi was resolved, this I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you remember who those three people were?

utterances.speaker: ZYMER HASANAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The three persons ... I don't remember. I don't remember at all who they were. I think maybe -- I'm just guessing: Xhevdet Krasniqi, Din, and someone else that I don't know. .

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When you said you heard that three people had gone to Ramush Haradinaj, did you hear that at the time -- at around the time that Din Krasniqi was made the commander?

utterances.speaker: ZYMER HASANAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Din Krasniqi became the commander and then of course we all suppose that this was done with the approval of Ramush. But I wasn't there. I didn't see anything. To speak the truth here, I wasn't there, present.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hasanaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any need to put further questions to the witness? Mr. Hasanaj, this concludes your evidence in this court. I would like to thank you for coming a long way to The Hague and to answer the questions of both parties and the Bench, and I wish you a safe trip home again. Madam Usher, could you escort Mr. Hasanaj out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to thank you, Your Honours. I would like to thank the International Tribunal and hope that justice will be done and that the innocent people will be redressed. If I am not doing anything wrong with the talk -- with the words I just said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What the Chamber would expect someone if justice is done, that the guilty will be punished and that those not guilty will be acquitted. That's what this Chamber, of course, is seeking to achieve. Thank you. I appreciate your words. You may follow Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, do I understand that your next witness is not yet available but will be available tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Professor Lecomte can only come tomorrow. She's testifying in a trial in Paris today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. We are not in a competition with French courts. That means that you have plenty of time to further see to agree with the Defence on the 92 ter statement for next Thursday, I take it. Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, I'll make it absolutely clear for the purposes of the record. I don't anticipate substantial measures of agreement, and I think all parties on this side of the room will be seeking a formal ruling from the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As far as, of course -- 92 ter statements, usually a decision is taken once they have been tendered. But the Chamber will certainly prepare for a -- for that situation, on the basis of the 92 ter statement and the annexes attached to it. It's quite a lot of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber is aware of that. We are doing our utmost best. And if the 7.00 in the morning sessions or 10.00 at night sessions would serve any purpose here, the Chamber will let you know, and in view of the amount of material, it might even be 9.00 in the evening or 6.00 in the morning sessions. I don't know. We have to --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I would just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- study it more thoroughly before we express any view on whether this would serve any purpose at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I would suggest that the present state of agreement between the parties, 4.00 in the morning might be more appropriate. I have a sneaking suspicion there's going to be no agreement here, Your Honour. Just so you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, I think, if I may say so, the reason why we chose to approach this in the formal way in which we did to the filing of the motion was because it raises an issue which has been skirted around in relation to a number of witnesses up until now where documents have been put forward and then withdrawn or put forward and clarification has been given that they're not being tendered as evidence of the truth of their contents but where the Prosecution has reserved the position that it may seek in due course to argue a different position. And -- and we do respectfully submit that this proposed evidence raises an issue of principle that needs to be formally resolved so that all parties can review the ruling and consider their position in the light of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I just want to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that. At the same time, I take it that the Defence is well aware by now that often the Chamber finds it premature to give final determinations on whether or not certain material is admissible because the evidence, of course, is viewed at in its entirety. And since the Chamber does not know what evidence there still will be there, that sometimes it's difficult to give a -- a final ruling already on admission, rather than --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- reserve the Chamber's position as to how to evaluate and how to give weight to that evidence. But we'll certainly --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: May --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: May I say that I think it should be reasonably apparent from the motion that in this particular instance, we're urging the Trial Chamber to take a more robust approach because we respectfully submit that it is possible and necessary to impose a measure of intellectual discipline over the basis upon which this material is sought to be tendered, because as it seems to us from the way in which the statement is put together and the annexes appended to it, this material must be being tendered, since no other reason is put forward, as being material that the Trial Chamber could and should in due course have available to it amongst the pool of material which is tendered as evidence of the truth of its contents, and we respectfully submit that that is not a permissible approach in respect of these materials and that is why, as I say, we -- we urge the Trial Chamber to look closely and invite the Prosecution to identify precisely the basis upon which each and every document is put forward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Emmerson, there could be no doubt as -- what is expressed in these 3.200 words in your submission. The Chamber is fully aware of that. We'll consider the matter. At the same time, Mr. Re, you are now aware of the objections raised. If this would lead you in any way to withdraw portions of the evidence -- I'm not suggesting that you would be inclined to do so, but if that would be the case, then, of course, it would assist the Chamber to be aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The Prosecution is, of course, always open to negotiation and -- and would, of course, take a reasonable course, but the Trial Chamber has to be very aware here. The louder the objection by the Defence to a statement and its annexes, the more likely it is to be incriminatory and relevant and provide persuasive evidence against the accused. In this particular case, the Defence have -- of Mr. Haradinaj, in any case have tendered or produced a 53-page filing going into great detail as to why what we say is highly relevant, probative and contemporaneous evidence against the three accused should not be tendered. Now, you've got to ask yourselves why they've gone to so much effort and trouble to try and suppress this relevant and probative evidence against the three accused. And the evidence here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let's try not to -- I take it that the Defence seeks to take care of the interest of the accused as good as they can, I mean, in these procedures.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, I take it one stage further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And any suggestion as to -- I mean, one of the things you did mention, Mr. Re -- but, of course, that seems to be not subject for negotiations but, rather, a matter of principle -- that is, reliability of evidence which cannot be tested. That's at least how I understand the position of the -- of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: As --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: We well understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The position is that everything which we have selected and put -- and attached to Mr. Stijovic's statement -- and let us not forget that he was the chief analyst for the Serbian Secret Service in Kosovo at the relevant time and they were receiving information from across Kosovo, from within the KLA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Et cetera. The reason why we have selected this particular information is because it is corroborative of the allegations in the indictment and of evidence the Trial Chamber has already heard. The objection the Defence is taking is as to their inability to test the maker of each of the statements in which some evidence is put in the -- in the annexes. Now, we -- we do, of course, recognise that, but we say that it is corroborative and once the pattern is built, there's a cumulative effect which when put together corroborates the Prosecution case. We, of course, understand that we cannot say that you can rely 100 per cent on everything in those annexes as the truth. However, when you take it with all the other pieces of information, the military orders, the statements, evidence you've heard in this -- in this trial, you can put it together. It has a cumulative effect, a corroborative effect, and the Trial Chamber can give it the appropriate weight. We don't say for one second that you can rely 100 per cent on everything that is in those statements. It's the jigsaw. It's the -- the pattern. It's putting it all together. And that's where we stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the positions are -- the positions are perfectly clear that --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I don't think it -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I don't think it -- nor did I contemplate that we were going to be arguing this motion at this time, but once again, based on the remarks just made by Mr. Re, I would urge him to define and articulate for the Chamber those annexes upon which the Prosecution relies on for purposes of their truth. I think that would, in many senses, be quite fruitful and quite helpful with regard to any potential negotiations that could occur independent of the underlying and important issues concerning what is reliable or not reliable from the standpoint of admissibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Might just briefly respond?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I don't seek the respond to the general point that Mr. Re sought to make that the making of objections by the Defence to material of this kind is somehow an indication that it is probative; quite the reverse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, don't worry about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No, I shan't -- I shan't, if I may say so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber is certainly in a position to interpret these kinds of observations, whether they come from the Defence or from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: But may I say simply this: That the remark that Mr. Re makes about corroboration is an excellent example of why this is essential that this matter be dealt with by a formal exchange of pleadings under ruling because I am aware because I have studied as much of the material as time has permitted, that there is material that is cited and relied upon there that is very far from being corroborative, that may relate to individuals who are named as victims on the indictment, but it provides in the Prosecution's case theory an explanation of the circumstances in which they allegedly met their death, which is quite absent from the testimony that can be tried and tested in these proceedings. And for the Trial Chamber to reach a judgement on admissibility of this material, there has, in our submission, to be an evaluation of its reliability and probative weight, and that's not something that one can do, unless or until the Prosecution properly responds and indicates how and why it says that, for example, a clutch of more than 10 or 12 records of interviews with anonymous witnesses or with named witnesses who are recorded as being unreliable is material on which the Trial Chamber can properly rely. And the general jigsaw puzzle suggestion is really An invitation to the Trial Chamber to say, Never mind the quality - feel the width, as the English expression goes. In other words, three unreliable indications together amount to a material on which the Prosecution can properly rely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, it's common knowledge that -- I'm not saying that it is, but a chain is as good as its weakest part.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I mean, my main concern is procedural here, is -- is that -- I entirely understand the general approach that the Trial Chamber takes to evaluating material at the end of the day, but there is -- the -- really the main thrust of Mr. Stijovic's proposed testimony is to come before the Tribunal and summarise witness statements, very few of which he says he saw at the time, none of which he took, and all of which he seeks to put forward before the Trial Chamber through summary form, as evidence of the truth of its contents. And we really do respectfully submit that a line needs now to be drawn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The positions are clear. Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yeah. Mr. Guy-Smith invited us to articulate and define the annexes of which the Prosecution relies on for the purposes of their truth. There are some which we clearly say we rely upon for their -- for their truth, such as every KLA communique in which they have admitted to murdering Serb collaborators and --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: There's no objection to the KLA communiques.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Now, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So there's a fruitful basis already for --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: But there is an objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I saw that --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The objection doesn't extend to those documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It says -- the objection, for example, says it does not, however, establish the authenticity of the alleged communique or the truth of the contents. We say it is true, and especially when Mr. Stijovic testifies in his statement, "Yes, I was there. I read reports at the time and in fact, I knew two of the people who were killed by the KLA in that particular incident." Of course we're putting that forward as a true communique issued by the KLA to say they killed people. Of course it is. And there's a lot of documents in that category.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I suggest that the parties, who have some additional time available this afternoon, try to find out to what extent there could be any agreement on whatever little matter. Of course, the Chamber would prefer larger matters, but -- and the Chamber will spend time as well on studying this material. This witness will appear on Thursday, which leaves us one day and a half to see to what extent the parties can resolve the matter, and what is not resolved by the parties but be resolved by the Chamber in whatever way. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. I wish to alert the Chamber to another issue that might arise. We have heard, I believe at least twice thus far, that Professor Lecomte is available for testimony only tomorrow as a result of being involved in another trial. We received yesterday a -- a fair amount of disclosure, some 600-plus pages of disclosure with regard to Professor Lecomte, of which 250, I believe, are in French. I don't know whether or not that is going to cause any difficulties with regard to the examination of Lecomte tomorrow or not. And by that I mean whether or not we may need to have her come back at a later time. However, I don't think we will have any difficulty, at least proceeding with her tomorrow. But I wanted to alert the Chamber that there may be a need for her to come back at a later time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's on the record. Then I would like to inform the parties before we adjourn that the Chamber at this moment is considering to have a housekeeping session on the 25th of October. That is, after the UN holiday on the 24th and the day before the 26th, a Friday, in which we usually do not sit. So the 25th, as far as the Chamber has in mind at this moment, would be reserved for a housekeeping session. If there's no other procedural matter, we'll resume until tomorrow, the 3rd of October, quarter past 2.00, same courtroom, number I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 3rd day of October, 2007, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 3.12 p.m.,
